clips.text_zh: 又係睇biz 巴打呻。其實佢講得啱，2020嗰陣唔識都贏，依家識都輸。prop firm 個p&L 仲紅緊。CFD 呢個月又輸多一注。算啦，當交學費🙏
clips.text_en_b1: It's impossible to get almost effortlessly rich on crypto like in 2020/21, 2017/16 and 2012/13. Nowadays it's just a casino with even more risk than a regular one. If you are making a lot of money, you were already loaded years ago, or you know the right people to get in early on rugpulls.
clips.text_en_b2: Getting effortlessly rich from crypto is essentially a thing of the past now, unlike the 2020-21 boom or earlier cycles where even clueless bagholders came out ahead. These days the market functions as little more than a casino, arguably riskier than a regulated one. Unless you were already wealthy or well-connected enough to front-run rugpulls, sustained profits remain out of reach. The past half-decade has produced nothing genuinely transformative, just the same recycled grift dressed up in fresh packaging. The original poster basically nailed it.
clips.text_en_c1: The effortless windfall era that defined earlier crypto cycles has effectively come to a close. Whereas ignorance itself was a viable strategy in 2017 or 2020, today's market resembles nothing so much as a casino whose odds have been deliberately stacked against retail participants. Those still extracting serious returns tend to fall into one of two camps: individuals who entered early enough to ride successive waves, or those with privileged access to pre-launch allocations and coordinated rugpulls. What is particularly telling is that, for half a decade now, no genuinely transformative protocol has emerged to reshape the landscape.
clips.text_en_c2: The consensus across /biz/ has hardened into something resembling resignation: the era when sheer ignorance could be monetised through cryptocurrency has, for all practical purposes, drawn to a close. Those who amassed fortunes during the parabolic runs of 2012–13, 2016–17, and 2020–21 did so not through perspicacity but through inadvertent timing, whereas today's market functions as a casino rigged against the retail participant, with leverage products and synthetic exposures guaranteeing that the house, as ever, prevails. One need only glance at the bleeding P&L statements emerging from proprietary trading firms this quarter to grasp the systemic nature of the attrition. No genuinely transformative protocol has surfaced in half a decade; what passes for innovation is merely old schemes reupholstered in fresh tokenomics.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ anon says crypto is now just a casino with more risk

clips.text_zh: 50% MSTR 50% SpaceX⋯⋯巴打你係咪食咗藥😅 我連prop firm challenge 都未過，仲話SpaceX。睇完當冇睇過，lol
clips.text_en_b1: The Sailor Moon strategy: 50% MSTR, 50% SpaceX. The plebs here aren't capable of conceiving such a powerful portfolio. MicroStrategy keeps buying Bitcoin while SpaceX keeps launching Starlink satellites, so the anon thinks holding both is the ultimate long-term play. Most anons will never get SpaceX exposure because it is still private.
clips.text_en_b2: Someone is pitching the Sailor Moon portfolio: fifty percent MicroStrategy and fifty percent SpaceX, because MSTR keeps accumulating Bitcoin while SpaceX keeps deploying Starlink satellites. The logic apparently is that this combination captures the ultimate long-term play across both assets. Most retail investors, however, cannot even get exposure to SpaceX since it remains private, so the entire thesis is essentially aspirational. Meanwhile, plenty of anons are still grinding away at prop firm challenges. The disconnect is genuinely staggering.
clips.text_en_c1: Dubbed the Sailor Moon strategy, this allocation pairs fifty percent MicroStrategy with fifty percent SpaceX, treating the former as a leveraged Bitcoin proxy while the latter provides exposure to Starlink's satellite constellation and adjacent revenue streams. The thesis is straightforward: if MicroStrategy keeps accumulating BTC and SpaceX keeps expanding orbital infrastructure, holding both constitutes the ultimate long-term position for those with sufficient conviction. The rub, as any seasoned observer will immediately note, is that retail investors have no viable pathway to SpaceX shares while the company remains private. Most participants, including those still struggling to clear proprietary firm challenges, are effectively locked out of half the portfolio.
clips.text_en_c2: What /biz/ has rather uncharitably dubbed the Sailor Moon portfolio — a fifty-fifty allocation between MicroStrategy and SpaceX — crystallises the gulf between retail imagination and institutional reality. The conceit, stripped of its memetic veneer, rests upon a superficially elegant thesis: MicroStrategy's relentless accumulation of Bitcoin functions as a leveraged proxy for the cryptocurrency complex, whereas SpaceX, through Starlink's commercial maturation, represents an analogous vehicle for the privatisation of orbital infrastructure. Whether this pairing constitutes the apotheosis of long-term positioning is, of course, a matter of temperament rather than analysis. The unpalatable truth, which the thread scrupulously avoids addressing, is that retail exposure to SpaceX remains functionally inaccessible while the company remains private, thereby rendering the strategy less an investment thesis than an exercise in aspirational cosplay.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ anon pitches 50/50 MSTR plus SpaceX portfolio

clips.text_zh: 外國人連上堂都傾Marx⋯⋯我哋做斜坡調查、soil nailing 邊有時間理。總之FE exam 唔考哲學，考factor of safety 就夠。
clips.text_en_b1: Snooze videos do not apply to reposts. Do you know what Karl Marx called Ferdinand Lassalle in a private letter? That is exactly what Elon Musk is. The thread on /g/ compares modern tech moguls to 19th century socialist drama, and anons keep pasting the same quote. Site engineers will never discuss this at a slope meeting.
clips.text_en_b2: Apparently some 4chan thread is comparing Elon Musk to Ferdinand Lassalle, citing a private letter where Karl Marx allegedly threw shade at his rival. The comparison is meant to highlight how modern tech moguls mirror nineteenth-century socialist drama, with the same ego clashes and ideological posturing. While anons keep reposting the quote for kicks, most practising engineers would find this completely irrelevant to their daily grind. Slope inspections, soil nailing reports, and factor-of-safety calculations leave zero room for philosophy.
clips.text_en_c1: There exists a particular irony in forum users reposting Karl Marx's famously caustic private remarks about Ferdinand Lassalle, applying them with apparent sincerity to contemporary technology magnates. Whether the analogy holds is, of course, a matter of considerable debate; what is indisputable is that the quote has acquired meme status on certain boards, where it circulates with metronomic regularity. Those who labour in more terrestrial disciplines, slope stabilisation, soil nailing investigations, the unglamorous arithmetic of factors of safety, will probably never encounter such discourse at a site meeting. The Fundamentals of Engineering examination, mercifully, makes no such philosophical demands.
clips.text_en_c2: The recent proliferation of /g/ threads drawing tendentious parallels between twenty-first century tech moguls and nineteenth-century socialist polemicists has, frankly, outstripped any reasonable appetite for historical analogy. The inciting incident appears to be Karl Marx's characteristically venomous private correspondence concerning Ferdinand Lassalle, in which the former trades insults that certain anons have deemed remarkably apposite to the present Silicon Valley moment. The juxtaposition is, admittedly, provocative — one can scarcely contest that the theatrical self-regard bears a family resemblance across centuries. Such considerations, however, occupy precisely zero cognitive bandwidth during a slope stability assessment or a soil nailing specification review. The Fundamentals of Engineering examination, mercifully, eschews political economy in favour of factors of safety and permissible bearing capacities, priorities which the conscientious geotechnical practitioner would do well to preserve.
clips.source_hint: /g/ anon compares Elon Musk to Lassalle from a Marx letter

clips.text_zh: 同我情況好似⋯⋯佢講75% job 都會畀AI 取代。我做GI report 都係照template 寫，遲早死🧐 唯有考牌走專業路線。wtf
clips.text_en_b1: Normies AI ignorance. Can anyone share what the normies in their lives think about AI? I mostly hear them regurgitate tabloid talking points about how data centres are loud and each prompt wastes a gallon of water. Meanwhile, I am seriously considering backup employment options after seeing firsthand that AI will be capable of automating away 75% of my job in the next year or…
clips.text_en_b2: Curious what ordinary people actually think about AI these days, because the consensus in my circle is depressingly shallow. They mostly parrot tabloid nonsense about data centres being noisy and each prompt allegedly guzzling a gallon of water, while brushing off the real implications entirely. Meanwhile, having witnessed firsthand how rapidly the technology is maturing, I am genuinely exploring backup career paths.
clips.text_en_c1: The chasm between public perception and professional reality regarding artificial intelligence has rarely been more pronounced. Acquaintances outside the industry tend to parrot tabloid talking points: the hum of server halls, the allegedly catastrophic water footprint per prompt, the spectre of sentient machines. Meanwhile, those of us whose daily output consists largely of templated deliverables recognise an altogether different threat. If current trajectories hold, roughly three-quarters of my role could feasibly be automated within the next eighteen months. GI reports, compliance documentation, formulaic client communications; all sit squarely in the crosshairs. The prudent response would appear to be credentialing, professional licensure, anything that confers a measure of defensibility.
clips.text_en_c2: The prevailing discourse among the technologically literate has shifted from speculative apprehension to something approaching anticipatory grief, as the obsolescence horizon for white-collar cognition contracts with each successive model release. What is particularly galling is the lacuna between public perception and professional reality: laypersons continue to circulate tabloid-inflected anxieties about the modest environmental footprint of inference, oblivious to the broader structural implications. Practitioners in cognitively templated disciplines — geotechnical reports, legal memoranda, routine medical correspondence — find themselves confronting an unpalatable calculus. If current trajectories hold, the proportion of cognitive labour susceptible to automation within the next biennium may plausibly approach seventy-five per cent.
clips.source_hint: /g/ anon worries AI will automate 75% of his job

clips.text_zh: lol 巴打話打機搞到少子化要禁game。我返工返到傻，邊有時間生仔，禁唔禁game 同我無關。ok 當笑話睇
clips.text_en_b1: Video game ban incoming. Vidya is destroying the birth rates, so the government is going to step in soon. Expect either an outright ban or something like in China, where you are allowed to play only a couple of hours per week. We need to get the youth away from the screens and back to work, the anon writes on /pol/.
clips.text_en_b2: Some /pol/ poster is convinced that video games are tanking birth rates, so the government will inevitably step in with restrictions, possibly mirroring China's model of limiting playtime to a couple of hours weekly. The argument is that gaming is keeping youth away from productive activities, hence the call for intervention. While the logic is entertaining, anyone working sixty-hour weeks barely has time to even glance at a screen, let alone raise a family. The whole debate feels entirely detached from reality.
clips.text_en_c1: The proposition that gaming is single-handedly precipitating a demographic collapse, and that legislative remedies are therefore imminent, has begun circulating with increasing frequency on certain boards. The proposed solutions range from outright prohibition to the rather more measured Chinese model, wherein minors are permitted a strictly rationed number of hours per week. For those of us consigned to the Sisyphean labour of contemporary office life, the entire debate carries a certain absurdist quality; reproductive ambitions have long since been subordinated to professional exhaustion, irrespective of any leisure activities that might occupy what remains of one's evenings. Whether the government intervenes or not, the outcome for this demographic seems largely predetermined.
clips.text_en_c2: The proposition advanced on /pol/ — that declining natalist indices can be attributed principally to adolescent immersion in interactive entertainment, and that statutory remedy is therefore imminent — illustrates with admirable precision the terminal disconnect between online discourse and lived economic reality. The demographic collapse afflicting industrialised economies stems from a concatenation of causes: stagnant real wages, housing unaffordability, the deferred adulthood hypothesis, and the generalised atomisation of contemporary social life, of which gaming constitutes at best a marginal accelerant. The breathless anticipation of prohibition, whether in the form of outright proscription or a Chinese-style rationing regime restricting minors to a token weekly allowance, betrays a touching faith in legislative efficacy. For the overworked wage-labourer scraping together survival between shifts, the prospect of fewer progeny emerges less from screens than from sheer exhaustion.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ anon predicts Western governments will ban video games for birthrate

clips.text_zh: 我squat 100kg、bench 80kg、deadlift 140kg，row 緊70kg。睇巴打傾我又要再谷。肥仔信今日又叫我返gym⋯⋯好喇今晚去🙏
clips.text_en_b1: How much do you barbell row? Compared to your squat, bench, and deadlift, how much are you repping out for barbell rows, and for how many reps? Most anons answer with a bodyweight ratio, then argue about whether rows should be heavy or just high reps for back thickness.
clips.text_en_b2: Curious what everyone is repping on barbell rows relative to their main lifts, because my current numbers feel a bit off. I am squatting around one hundred kilos, benching eighty, and pulling one-forty on deadlifts, yet my rows are stuck at roughly seventy kilos, which seems disproportionately low. The old-school consensus seems to be that anything below sixty percent of your deadlift indicates a lagging posterior chain, so apparently I have work to do. The gym awaits tonight, whether I like it or not.
clips.text_en_c1: The barbell row occupies an oddly contentious position within the broader pantheon of compound lifts, and the question of how heavily one ought to load it provokes considerable disagreement among experienced trainees. A typical exchange sees participants citing their current squat, bench, and deadlift figures before proffering row weights, usually expressed as a percentage of bodyweight or of their deadlift. The consensus, insofar as one exists, suggests that rows performed below sixty percent of one's deadlift capacity indicate a posterior chain that is materially under-developed relative to the rest of the physique. Veterans therefore advocate either heavier loading or substantially higher rep ranges to remedy the discrepancy.
clips.text_en_c2: The perennial /fit/ disputation concerning barbell row loading has resurfaced with its customary vehemence, occasioned by a thread soliciting quantitative ratios relative to squat, bench, and deadlift maxima. The emergent consensus, such as it is, holds that posterior chain development ought to be calibrated against one's deadlift capacity, with row tonnage falling somewhere in the vicinity of forty to sixty per cent of that figure depending on individual leverages and stylistic preferences. Traditionalists of the Ted Arcissi school insist that anything appreciably below the lower threshold indicates systemic neglect of the spinal erectors and rhomboids, whereas the hypertrophy-minded contingent advocates lighter loads pushed through voluminous repetition schemes in pursuit of capillary density and that elusive quality known as back thickness.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread asking about barbell row numbers vs squat/bench/deadlift

clips.text_zh: Demon Slayer 第一⋯⋯我認。劇場版入場排到癲。Gintama 都係我至愛。睇完好返去溫書，FE exam 等我👍
clips.text_en_b1: Cultural impact ranking of manga and anime franchises. 1. Demon Slayer - simply the biggest phenomenon, no explanation needed. 2. Gintama - birthed Demon Slayer's style. 3. Bleach - birthed many things. 4. Black Clover - birthed by Bleach. 5. Kagurabachi. The thread on /a/ argues these series overwrote even some minor celebrities like Michael Jackson in pure global reach.
clips.text_en_b2: Ranking franchises by pure cultural footprint, Demon Slayer clearly takes the top spot, since the phenomenon needs little introduction given how thoroughly it dominated both box offices and streaming charts. Gintama earns second place for essentially birthing the style Demon Slayer later perfected, while Bleach comes third for spawning countless imitators. Black Clover slots into fourth, owing its DNA directly to its predecessor, with Kagurabachi rounding out the list. Collectively, these series have arguably eclipsed even major celebrities in raw global reach.
clips.text_en_c1: Any attempt to rank the cultural footprint of contemporary manga and anime franchises is, by its very nature, an exercise in provocation, yet certain hierarchies have acquired the status of received wisdom. Demon Slayer occupies the apex: its theatrical releases have generated queues of a length typically reserved for the most fevered cultural moments, and its global penetration has, by certain metrics, eclipsed that of established celebrities. Gintama, Bleach, and Black Clover each represent successive waves of stylistic influence, a lineage that culminates, perhaps inevitably, in the curious phenomenon of Kagurabachi.
clips.text_en_c2: The /a/ consensus ranking of contemporary manga and anime franchises by cultural footprint — a metric which, however imprecise, captures something real about global penetration — places Demon Slayer at the apex, a verdict difficult to dispute given its capacity to generate box-office queues of genuinely unprecedented length and to function as a gateway property for an entire generation of previously indifferent consumers. Gintama's second-place positioning reflects its stylistic paternity, insofar as its tonal blend of histrionic parody and sincere melodrama arguably established the template that Demon Slayer subsequently inherited and refined. Bleach, Black Clover, and Kagurabachi complete the hierarchy, each linked to its predecessor by formal genealogy.
clips.source_hint: /a/ thread ranking manga/anime by cultural impact, top is Demon Slayer
